1.q: Which sequence is safest before starting work from a scaffold?
o: Check tag, inspect access, assess platform, then begin
Load materials, then inspect while working
Climb first, ask questions later
Remove rails for easier movement, then start
Start with urgent tasks and inspect afterwards
1.w: Inspection status, safe access and platform condition should be checked before use.

n.1: Loading first can worsen unsafe conditions.
n.2: Checks should happen before climbing.
n.3: Removing rails creates hazards.
n.4: Urgency does not replace pre-use checks.

1.q: You are asked to use a trolley to move blocks across site. One wheel is loose and wobbles badly. What should you do?
o: Report the defect and use another safe trolley if available
Use it slowly for one trip only
Ask a workmate to steady the load while moving
Carry more blocks so fewer trips are needed
Use it only on smooth ground
1.w: Workers should use equipment properly and report defective equipment before use.

n.1: A single trip with defective equipment can still cause injury.
n.2: Extra help does not remove the defect.
n.3: Increasing the load may worsen the risk.
n.4: Surface condition does not fix the faulty wheel.

1.q: What is the best sequence before entering a marked noisy zone?
o: Inspect hearing PPE, fit it, then enter
Enter first, then look for ear plugs
Wait inside until noise starts
Ask others later if protection is needed
Take PPE off to hear instructions
1.w: Protection should be fitted before exposure begins.

n.1: You may already be exposed before fitting it.
n.2: Waiting inside increases exposure risk.
n.3: Requirements should be known before entry.
n.4: Removing PPE increases risk in the zone.

1.q: You see a small fire starting in a bin and nobody else is nearby. What should happen first?
o: Raise the alarm and alert others
Move the bin deeper inside
Ignore it if it is small
Wait for smoke detectors only
Take photos for evidence
1.w: The first priority is to warn others and activate the emergency response.

n.1: Moving a burning bin can spread fire or injure you.
n.2: Even small fires can grow quickly.
n.3: Do not rely solely on automatic systems.
n.4: Recording events is not the priority during a fire.

1.q: Which yellow triangle symbol most likely warns about movement of plant equipment?
o: Forklift truck
Green cross
Red flame bar
Blue hard hat
White arrow
1.w: Vehicle symbols in yellow triangles warn of moving plant.

n.1: Green cross indicates first aid.
n.2: Not the standard plant warning format.
n.3: Blue hard hat is mandatory PPE.
n.4: Arrows give direction, not plant hazard.

1.q: Which situation most clearly suggests using a trolley instead of carrying by hand?
o: Several medium boxes need moving the same route
One light folder needs moving five metres
An empty bag needs moving once
A single glove is on the floor
A small tool is already in your pocket
1.w: Repeated movement of several boxes is where a trolley gives clear benefit.

n.1: A very light single item may not justify a trolley.
n.2: A single empty bag may not need mechanical aid.
n.3: This does not require transport equipment.
n.4: No movement aid is needed.

1.q: When should you report an accident to your supervisor?
o: As soon as possible after it happens
Only at the weekly meeting
When someone asks later
At the end of the year
Only if you need compensation
1.w: Prompt reporting allows treatment, control measures and accurate records.

n.1: Waiting for meetings can delay action.
n.2: Reporting should not depend on being asked.
n.3: This is far too late.
n.4: Reporting is for safety and compliance, not only claims.

1.q: You get cement on your hands after removing gloves. What next?
o: Ignore it
Wash with clean water and mild cleanser promptly
Eat first
Rub with fuel
Use sandpaper
1.w: Prompt washing removes residue and reduces irritation.

n.0: Ignoring residue can harm skin.
n.2: Eating before washing risks contamination.
n.3: Fuel can damage skin further.
n.4: Abrasion may worsen injury.

1.q: You are asked to finish one last cut with a lead that has a damaged outer sheath. What is the best response?
o: Refuse to use it and report the defect
Use it once because the cut is short
Rest the damaged section on timber first
Ask someone else to stand by
Switch hands halfway through
1.w: A damaged lead should not be used for even one more task. The correct action is to refuse use and report it.

n.1: Task duration does not reduce the electrical hazard.
n.2: Supporting the cable does not repair the damage.
n.3: Having someone nearby does not make unsafe equipment safe.
n.4: Hand changes do not address the defect.

1.q: You are carrying materials along a walkway and approach a crossing point. What should you do?
o: Keep going because the load gives you priority
Pause, check traffic and cross only when safe
Cross behind the nearest vehicle
Put the load down in the road first
Step around barriers to shorten the route
1.w: Loads can restrict vision and movement, so pause and cross only when safe.

n.0: Loads do not give priority.
n.2: Crossing behind vehicles is hazardous.
n.3: Leaving materials in the road creates hazards.
n.4: Going around barriers defeats route controls.

1.q: A delivery vehicle must pass near an excavation. What should happen before it moves close to the edge?
o: Remove the fencing.
Let the driver judge it.
Keep pedestrians back and control the vehicle movement.
Ask workers to stand at the excavation edge and watch.
Allow the vehicle through quickly before the route gets busy.
1.w: Vehicle movement near an excavation should be controlled so people are kept away and the vehicle does not approach the edge unsafely.

n.0: Removing fencing increases the risk of falls.
n.1: Driver judgement alone is not enough near an excavation edge.
n.3: Standing at the edge exposes workers to unnecessary danger.
n.4: Rushing the movement increases risk rather than reducing it.

1.q: You see fuel flowing toward a surface drain after a small spill. What should you do first?
o: Leave it because the drain will dilute it.
Wait for the supervisor to notice it.
Push it faster into the drain with water.
Walk away and return later.
Block the drain if safe and use spill controls immediately.
1.w: Stopping pollution entering the drain is the priority, using safe containment methods and spill materials.

n.0: Drains can carry pollution directly into water systems.
n.1: Immediate action is needed.
n.2: Water can spread contamination faster.
n.3: Leaving it unmanaged increases damage.

1.q: You notice the site drinking water container is empty on a hot day. What is the best action?
o: Ignore it and keep working.
Use water from a cleaning bucket.
Report it so drinking water is replenished.
Drink from a nearby puddle.
Wait until the shift ends.
1.w: A supply of drinking water is an important welfare provision and shortages should be addressed promptly.

n.0: Workers still need access to drinking water.
n.1: Cleaning water may be unsuitable to drink.
n.3: Unsafe water can cause illness.
n.4: Delay may risk dehydration.

1.q: Why are drugs or alcohol a serious safety risk on site?
o: They improve reaction times.
They can impair judgement and coordination.
They make PPE unnecessary.
They only affect office staff.
They reduce all hazards automatically.
1.w: Drugs or alcohol can reduce judgement, concentration, balance and reaction time.

n.0: Impairment usually worsens reactions.
n.2: PPE is still required.
n.3: Anyone can be affected.
n.4: They increase rather than remove risk.

1.q: A leaning ladder is set one metre away from the wall and reaches four metres up. What does that usually mean?
o: The angle is about right
The ladder is much too shallow for safe use
The ladder is nearly vertical and likely to tip backwards
The ladder must be reclassified before it can be used
The ladder is only suitable if another worker stands at the bottom
1.w: A one-out to four-up ratio is the usual guide for a leaning ladder angle.

n.1: A shallow ladder would normally have the feet further away from the wall.
n.2: A near-vertical ladder would normally have the feet much closer to the wall.
n.3: Correct angle does not create any need for reclassification.
n.4: Someone standing at the bottom is not what this ratio indicates.

1.q: Why should damaged PPE be reported quickly?
o: It may no longer protect the wearer properly
It improves overtime chances
It reduces paperwork
It guarantees a pay rise
It avoids needing training
1.w: Damaged PPE may fail when needed and should be replaced or repaired.

n.1: Reporting PPE damage is unrelated to overtime.
n.2: Reporting may create paperwork rather than reduce it.
n.3: There is no link to pay rises.
n.4: Training needs remain separate.

1.q: What is the best sequence before entering a dusty area with a respirator?
o: Enter area, tighten straps, then check fit.
Fit respirator, carry out fit check, then enter.
Enter area first, then read instructions later.
Put on gloves only, then enter.
Hold breath, then adjust inside area.
1.w: The respirator should be fitted and checked before entering the hazardous area.

n.0: Entering first may expose you before protection is confirmed.
n.2: Instructions should be understood before exposure.
n.3: Gloves do not replace respiratory PPE.
n.4: Adjusting inside the area increases exposure.

1.q: What is the best location for storing mixed fuels and gas cylinders together?
o: Anywhere indoors
Inside welfare cabins
Separate designated storage areas with suitable controls
In stairwells
Under scaffolds only
1.w: Different hazardous materials should be stored in controlled designated areas with suitable separation.

n.0: General indoor storage is unsuitable.
n.1: Welfare cabins are inappropriate.
n.3: Stairwells must remain clear.
n.4: Under scaffolds is not automatically suitable.

1.q: Which statement about fire exit routes is correct?
o: They may be used for storage if access remains narrow
They should be kept clear at all times
They can be locked during working hours
They are only needed after normal shifts
They are for managers first
1.w: Escape routes must remain clear and usable at all times.

n.0: Any storage can obstruct or slow evacuation.
n.2: Routes must be readily openable in an emergency.
n.3: Emergencies can happen at any time.
n.4: Exits are for everyone on site.

1.q: You are lifting paving blocks from uneven ground. What should you do first?
o: Check your footing is stable before lifting
Lift quickly before balance changes
Keep feet close together to save space
Twist toward the stack as you lift
Lean back to counter the weight
1.w: Stable footing helps maintain balance and control during the lift.

n.1: Speed does not replace safe preparation.
n.2: Feet close together reduces stability.
n.3: Twisting while lifting is unsafe.
n.4: Leaning back can destabilise the lift.

1.q: What usually comes first after witnessing a near miss if there is immediate danger?
o: Warn others and make the area safe if possible
Complete paperwork before speaking to anyone
Go home and report tomorrow
Post about it on social media
Restart the task immediately
1.w: Where immediate danger exists, preventing harm is the first priority before formal reporting.

n.1: Paperwork should not come before urgent safety action.
n.2: Delay is inappropriate.
n.3: Public posting does not control risk.
n.4: Restarting work without controls is unsafe.

1.q: A co-worker says labels are only needed for managers. What is the best response?
o: Agree if workers are experienced
Explain everyone using or moving chemicals must understand labels
Ignore the comment
Remove labels to save time
Use verbal warnings only
1.w: Anyone exposed to or handling hazardous substances needs label information.

n.0: Experience does not replace hazard communication.
n.2: Unsafe misunderstandings should be corrected.
n.3: Removing labels increases risk.
n.4: Verbal warnings alone are unreliable.

1.q: What should you do if cable plans are unclear or missing?
o: Guess where services are and start carefully
Stop and obtain proper information before digging
Use the largest bucket available
Dig faster to reduce time exposed
Ignore plans and rely only on luck
1.w: If plans are unclear or unavailable, work should not proceed until proper information is obtained.

n.0: Guessing buried service locations is unsafe.
n.2: Large buckets increase strike risk.
n.3: Speed does not remove uncertainty.
n.4: Luck is not a control measure.

1.q: Why should a driver follow one banksman only?
o: It reduces confusion and keeps control of the vehicle movement clear
It allows the vehicle to reverse without mirrors
It means pedestrians can enter the route
It removes the need for reversing alarms
It lets anyone nearby give extra signals
1.w: Following one authorised banksman prevents conflicting instructions and keeps movement controlled.

n.1: Mirrors and visibility aids may still be needed.
n.2: Pedestrians must still stay clear of danger zones.
n.3: Reversing alarms may still be required.
n.4: Extra signals can confuse the driver.

1.q: Cones have been placed near an excavation edge, but people can still walk between them. What does this suggest?
o: The cones are enough.
The excavation is low risk.
The area only needs signs.
The controls may not prevent access to the danger area.
The cones should be removed so the edge is easier to see.
1.w: If people can walk through the control and reach the edge, the setup may not properly prevent access to the danger area.

n.0: Cones are not enough if they allow easy access to the edge.
n.1: An accessible excavation edge remains a significant risk.
n.2: Signs alone do not stop people entering the danger area.
n.4: Removing cones would reduce control even further.

1.q: You have leftover paint tins containing liquid paint. Where should they go?
o: In the wood skip.
In the mixed recycling skip.
In the designated hazardous waste container.
Into the nearest empty general skip.
Left open to dry beside the fence.
1.w: Paint and similar chemical residues often require disposal as hazardous waste in designated containers.

n.0: Wood skips are for timber waste, not paint tins with residue.
n.1: Liquid paint contamination can spoil recycling loads.
n.3: General skips may be unsuitable and non-compliant.
n.4: Leaving waste unsecured can cause spills and pollution.

1.q: You are about to use a very noisy cut-off saw. What should you do first?
o: Wear suitable hearing protection.
Start quickly before others arrive.
Use cotton wool instead.
Ignore the noise for short jobs.
Stand farther away while cutting.
1.w: Noisy tools can damage hearing, so suitable hearing protection should be worn before use.

n.1: Starting quickly does not reduce hearing risk.
n.2: Cotton wool is not suitable hearing protection.
n.3: Short exposure can still contribute to damage.
n.4: Distance alone may not provide enough protection while operating the tool.

1.q: You are taking medication that may cause drowsiness before a shift. What should you do?
o: Take extra caffeine and continue normally.
Use only ladders and low-risk tasks.
Say nothing if it is prescribed.
Wait until you feel worse before mentioning it.
Check fitness for work and report any safety concern.
1.w: Some medication can affect alertness, so fitness for work should be checked and concerns reported.

n.0: Caffeine does not guarantee safe alertness.
n.1: Even low-risk tasks can become unsafe when drowsy.
n.2: Prescribed medication can still affect safety.
n.3: Concerns should be raised before work creates risk.

1.q: A co-worker says any strong steel can be used as an anchor. What is the best response?
o: Agree if it is thicker than the lanyard
Use only approved anchor points identified for the task
Use it if another worker has done so before
Use it for restraint but not for fall arrest
Agree if the beam has no rust
1.w: Anchors must be suitable and approved for the task, not chosen by appearance.

n.0: Thickness alone does not prove suitability.
n.2: Previous misuse does not make it safe.
n.3: Use type still requires approved anchorage.
n.4: Rust condition alone is not the deciding factor.

1.q: Which welfare facility is most appropriate for meal breaks on many sites?
o: A rest area with somewhere to sit and eat
A vehicle cab parked outside
Standing in the materials store
Eating beside cutting operations
Using the toilet area as a canteen
1.w: Suitable rest facilities should be available for breaks.

n.1: Vehicle cabs are not normally suitable welfare areas.
n.2: Stores may be unsafe or unsuitable.
n.3: Eating beside dusty or noisy work is inappropriate.
n.4: Toilet areas are unsuitable for meals.

1.q: A worker removes his hard hat because it is hot while walking through a scaffolded access route. What is the error?
o: Removing head protection inside a designated risk area
Walking too slowly through the route
Using the main access route instead of another path
Speaking to other workers while walking
Wearing hi-vis clothing with the helmet off
1.w: Comfort does not justify removing required PPE in a hazard zone.

n.1: Walking speed is not the key issue here.
n.2: The route itself is not necessarily wrong.
n.3: Conversation is secondary to PPE non-compliance.
n.4: Hi-vis use does not compensate for missing head protection.

1.q: A co-worker says the alarm is probably false, so stay put. What should you do?
o: Evacuate unless instructed otherwise
Agree and keep working
Wait for smoke to appear
Silence the alarm yourself
Go for a break instead
1.w: Treat alarms seriously and evacuate unless authorised staff advise otherwise.

n.1: Ignoring alarms is unsafe.
n.2: Smoke may appear too late.
n.3: Only authorised persons should handle alarm systems.
n.4: A break is not an emergency response.

1.q: What should you assume if a mandatory PPE sign remains in place but work appears quiet?
o: The requirement still applies unless changed
PPE can be ignored during breaks
Signs only matter when machines run
Visitors may decide themselves
Rules stop after lunch
1.w: Follow site signage until authorised changes are made.

n.1: Break times do not automatically cancel controls.
n.2: Residual hazards may remain.
n.3: Visitors must also follow relevant controls.
n.4: There is no automatic lunch exemption.

1.q: Which sequence is safest when lifting a box from the floor?
o: Stable feet, bend knees, grip close, lift with legs
Grip quickly, pull with arms, then step back
Feet together, bend back, stand fast
Twist first, then straighten legs sharply
Lift one side first, then balance it
1.w: This order creates balance, good posture and controlled lifting force.

n.1: Pulling with arms first is poor technique.
n.2: Feet together and bending the back are unsafe.
n.3: Twisting and sharp movement increase risk.
n.4: Lifting unevenly can destabilise the load.

1.q: What should come first after witnessing a serious incident with ongoing danger?
o: Raise the alarm and make the area safe if possible
Complete the accident book before acting
Take photos for social media
Resume nearby work quickly
Discuss blame with colleagues
1.w: Immediate protection of people and emergency response takes priority.

n.1: Paperwork comes after urgent safety actions.
n.2: Photos are not the priority.
n.3: Restarting work may be dangerous.
n.4: Blame discussions do not control risk.

1.q: A bottle has been poured into a drink container for convenience. What is the main problem?
o: It looks untidy
It may be mistaken for a drink and lacks proper hazard labelling
It is lighter to carry
It saves storage space
It is easier to refill
1.w: Using food or drink containers creates confusion and removes proper hazard communication.

n.0: Appearance is not the main risk.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant to the hazard.
n.3: Space saving does not justify unsafe storage.
n.4: Convenience does not remove the danger.

1.q: What is the main risk if a lead is frayed and copper conductors are exposed?
o: It may make the tool louder
It may reduce battery life
It can cause electric shock or short circuit
It makes storage untidy
It may change the tool speed slightly
1.w: Exposed conductors can cause electric shock, short circuit, burns, or fire.

n.0: Noise is not the main danger from exposed conductors.
n.1: This is about mains cable safety, not battery performance.
n.3: Untidiness is minor compared with the electrical hazard.
n.4: Speed change is not the main safety concern.

1.q: Which sequence is safest before crossing a vehicle route on site?
o: Cross, look, listen, wave, run
Look, make sure drivers see you, use crossing point, cross when clear, keep watching
Wave, step out, listen, stop, cross
Listen, run, look, stop, cross
Wait, turn away, cross, look, stop
1.w: Check the route, confirm visibility, use the proper crossing point and continue observing while crossing.

n.0: Crossing before checking is unsafe.
n.2: Stepping out early is dangerous.
n.3: Running and late checks are poor practice.
n.4: Turning away removes awareness.

1.q: What is the main purpose of a confined space entry permit?
o: To record wages for the shift.
To replace the need for supervision.
To show who owns the equipment.
To confirm hazards, controls and authorisation for entry.
To guarantee no danger remains.
1.w: A permit confirms identified hazards, required controls, checks and authorised entry arrangements.

n.0: A permit is not a payroll record.
n.1: Supervision may still be required.
n.2: Ownership of equipment is not its main purpose.
n.4: A permit manages risk but does not guarantee zero danger.

1.q: A skip is clearly labelled for plasterboard only. What should you do with broken bricks?
o: Put them in anyway if there is space.
Hide them underneath plasterboard sheets.
Use the correct skip for masonry or mixed inert waste.
Leave them on the ground beside the skip.
Break them smaller and add them later.
1.w: Waste should go into the correctly labelled skip to avoid contamination and extra disposal cost.

n.0: Available space does not override segregation rules.
n.1: Concealing contamination is unacceptable.
n.3: Loose waste beside skips creates housekeeping issues.
n.4: Changing size does not make it the correct waste type.

1.q: Toilet facilities are blocked and unusable. What should happen?
o: Nothing until next week.
Use any quiet corner outside.
Keep working and avoid drinking water.
Share a storage container instead.
Report it so facilities are cleaned or repaired quickly.
1.w: Unusable toilets should be reported promptly so suitable welfare provision is restored.

n.0: Delays leave inadequate welfare arrangements.
n.1: Improvised toileting is unhygienic and unacceptable.
n.2: Avoiding water is not a safe solution.
n.3: Storage containers are not toilet facilities.

1.q: A coworker keeps throwing small items across the site for fun. What is the best action?
o: Throw them back.
Laugh and carry on working.
Tell them to stop and report it if it continues.
Move closer so you can catch them.
Hide the items and say nothing.
1.w: Throwing objects is unsafe and can injure others. It should be challenged and reported if it continues.

n.0: Throwing items back escalates the risk.
n.1: Ignoring unsafe acts allows them to continue.
n.3: Moving closer increases your risk of injury.
n.4: Silence does not address the unsafe behaviour.

1.q: Which condition would most likely make a ladder foot slip?
o: Wet or contaminated ground surface
A visible serial number label
Using both side rails
Facing the ladder while climbing
Keeping hands free of tools
1.w: Wet, oily or contaminated ground can reduce friction at the feet.

n.1: Labels do not affect slip resistance.
n.2: Using side rails is normal.
n.3: Facing the ladder is good practice.
n.4: Free hands improve climbing safety.

1.q: You notice a trailing extension lead across a walkway. What should you do?
o: Report it and make the area safe if you can do so safely
Step over it and continue your task
Ignore it because it belongs to another trade
Wait to see if anyone trips first
Pull it sharply out of the socket
1.w: Trip hazards should be addressed promptly through safe action and reporting.

n.1: Personal avoidance leaves risk for others.
n.2: Hazards should not be ignored due to trade boundaries.
n.3: Waiting allows preventable incidents.
n.4: Unsafe removal may create electrical danger.

1.q: The shell of your hard hat has become brittle after long sun exposure in storage. What should you do?
o: Replace it because environmental ageing can reduce protection
Use it until visible cracks appear during work
Cover it with tape to block sunlight
Only wear it in winter months
Drill vents into it to relieve stress
1.w: UV and ageing can degrade plastics and weaken helmets.

n.1: Waiting for failure signs can be unsafe.
n.2: Tape does not reverse material degradation.
n.3: Seasonal use does not solve brittleness.
n.4: Drilling holes damages the shell further.

1.q: You discover a live electrical cabinet smoking with flames visible. What is the best action if trained and escape is clear?
o: Use a CO2 extinguisher
Use a water extinguisher
Open the cabinet fully first
Use foam directly into vents
Throw sand onto cables
1.w: CO2 is commonly used for electrical fires because it does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue.

n.1: Water can conduct electricity and may cause shock.
n.2: Opening the cabinet can feed the fire with oxygen.
n.3: Foam may not be suitable on live electrical equipment.
n.4: Sand is not the preferred controlled response for this situation.

1.q: You are closest to a fire exit but it opens into visible flames outside. What should you do?
o: Use that exit quickly anyway
Choose another safe signed escape route
Stay inside and keep working
Break a window immediately
Return for belongings first
1.w: Use the nearest safe exit. If one route is unsafe, use another signed route.

n.0: Do not move into obvious danger.
n.2: You still need to evacuate.
n.3: Breaking windows is not the normal first action.
n.4: Do not delay for belongings.

1.q: You are lowering a heavy item to the floor. What should you do?
o: Bend your knees and keep the load close as you lower it
Drop it from knee height once you are tired
Lean forward with straight legs to reach down
Twist and place it beside you in one motion
Push it away from your body before lowering
1.w: Lowering with bent knees and the load close mirrors safe lifting technique.

n.1: Dropping a load can cause loss of control or damage.
n.2: Straight-leg leaning strains the back.
n.3: Twisting while lowering is unsafe.
n.4: Pushing away increases leverage and strain.

1.q: You notice sparks from damaged temporary lighting but no fire starts. What is the best action?
o: Report it immediately and keep clear if unsafe
Carry on because power is still working
Touch the fitting to check heat level
Wait until the shift ends to mention it
Cover it with cloth to stop sparks
1.w: Electrical defects creating sparks are serious near miss hazards and need immediate reporting.

n.1: Working equipment can still be dangerous.
n.2: Touching damaged electrics is unsafe.
n.3: Delay may allow fire or shock risk to continue.
n.4: Improvised coverings can worsen the hazard.

1.q: Why should gloves be checked before handling cement?
o: For colour
To make sure they are intact and not leaking
To weigh them
To warm them
To fold them
1.w: Damaged gloves may allow wet cement onto the skin.

n.0: Colour does not provide protection.
n.2: Weight is irrelevant.
n.3: Warmth is not the main purpose.
n.4: Folding is irrelevant.

2.q: You need both hands briefly to tighten a fitting while on a ladder. What should you do to maintain stability?
o: Keep three points of contact as much as possible and pause if you cannot
Stand on the top rung to get closer
Lean your body sideways to reach faster
Hold tools in one hand while climbing
Jump down once the fitting is tight
2.w: Three points of contact should be maintained whenever possible; if not, reassess the method.

n.1: Top rungs are not intended as standing positions.
n.2: Leaning sideways increases the chance of overturning.
n.3: Carrying tools by hand while climbing reduces safe contact points.
n.4: Jumping from ladders creates avoidable injury risk.

2.q: Which order is best when you find unsafe equipment?
o: Stop use, isolate if possible, report it
Use it, clean it, report later
Lend it out, then inspect it
Repair it secretly, then continue
Ignore it until break time
2.w: Unsafe equipment should be stopped from use and reported promptly.

n.1: Using defective equipment can cause injury.
n.2: Passing on unsafe equipment increases risk.
n.3: Unauthorised repairs may be unsafe.
n.4: Delays can expose others to harm.

2.q: You cannot read the manufacturing or expiry marking on your hard hat. What is the best action?
o: Report it and obtain one with legible markings
Assume it is fine if it still fits well
Write any date on it yourself
Use it only on short shifts
Keep using it until a supervisor notices
2.w: Unreadable markings prevent proper checks on service life and traceability.

n.1: Fit alone does not confirm compliance or age.
n.2: Self-marking false dates is unacceptable.
n.3: Shorter use does not solve the issue.
n.4: Known defects should be acted on immediately.

2.q: Where should petrol for site equipment normally be stored?
o: In an approved locked flammable store
Under the stairs for quick access later
Beside a heater to keep it warm
Inside the canteen cupboard overnight
Next to batteries for convenience
2.w: Flammable liquids should be kept in approved secure stores designed to reduce fire risk.

n.1: Stairs and escape routes must be kept clear and free from fuel hazards.
n.2: Heat sources increase vapour and ignition risk.
n.3: Canteen areas are unsuitable for fuel storage.
n.4: Fuel should be separated from ignition and electrical risks.

2.q: Which sign most clearly bans an action rather than warning of a hazard?
o: A red circle with a slash over a cigarette
A yellow triangle with a lightning bolt
A blue circle with a hard hat
A green sign showing first aid
A white directional arrow
2.w: A red circle with a slash is a prohibition sign and bans the action shown.

n.1: This is a warning sign that alerts you to electrical danger.
n.2: This is a mandatory sign requiring an action.
n.3: This provides safe-condition information rather than a ban.
n.4: A directional arrow does not prohibit an action.

2.q: Which load is most likely to require team lifting?
o: A long pipe that is hard to balance
A small toolbox with handles
An empty bucket
A folded warning sign
A short plastic tray
2.w: Long awkward loads may be difficult to balance and control alone.

n.1: A small handled toolbox may be suitable for one person.
n.2: An empty bucket is usually manageable alone.
n.3: A folded sign is often light and compact.
n.4: A short tray is less awkward than a long pipe.

2.q: What is the main purpose of an accident book?
o: To keep an official record of workplace accidents
To list holiday requests
To store toolbox talk notes only
To record deliveries only
To replace first-aid treatment
2.w: An accident book provides a formal record of incidents and injuries.

n.1: Holiday requests are unrelated.
n.2: Toolbox talks are separate records.
n.3: Deliveries use other systems.
n.4: Recording does not replace treatment.

2.q: Which location is best for cutting dusty materials where possible?
o: A small sealed room
A well-ventilated area with controls in place
Busy pedestrian walkway
Inside welfare cabin
Near stored food
2.w: Where possible, dusty tasks should be done in well-ventilated controlled areas.

n.0: A sealed room can trap dust.
n.2: This exposes others.
n.3: Welfare areas are unsuitable.
n.4: Food areas should be kept free from contamination.

2.q: When services are expected in the ground, what is commonly done near the marked route?
o: Use careful hand digging or controlled methods
Drive plant harder into the area
Ignore markings if no sparks appear
Use only reverse gear nearby
Pour water to reveal cables
2.w: Near suspected service routes, careful hand digging or other controlled methods are commonly used.

n.1: Aggressive digging increases strike risk.
n.2: No sparks does not mean no buried cable.
n.3: Direction of travel is not the control.
n.4: Water is not a normal locating method.

2.q: Which action should a pedestrian take when a banksman is controlling a vehicle movement?
o: Walk behind the banksman to pass quickly
Stay outside the controlled area until the movement is complete
Follow the banksman's signals as if they were for pedestrians
Cross when the vehicle is moving slowly
Stand near the driver to be seen
2.w: Pedestrians should stay out of the controlled vehicle movement area unless told it is safe.

n.0: Walking behind the banksman may still enter the danger zone.
n.2: The signals are intended for the driver, not for pedestrians to enter.
n.3: Slow movement can still cause serious injury.
n.4: Standing near the driver may put you close to moving plant.

2.q: Why should trenches be inspected regularly during work?
o: To count tools each hour
Because ground conditions can change and create new hazards
To make workers slower
To reduce the need for ladders
To keep spoil heaps wetter
2.w: Weather, vibration and time can change trench stability, so regular checks are important.

n.0: Tool counts are not the main reason.
n.2: Inspections are for safety, not delay.
n.3: Ladders may still be needed.
n.4: Moisture control is not the main reason.

2.q: A fuel bowser is being used on uneven ground. What is the main environmental concern?
o: It may spill if unstable or poorly controlled.
It will automatically hold more fuel.
It becomes easier to repaint.
It stops all vapours forming.
It needs no supervision.
2.w: Unstable refuelling setups can increase the chance of spills or hose problems.

n.1: Ground level does not increase capacity.
n.2: Repainting is irrelevant.
n.3: Uneven ground does not remove vapours.
n.4: Supervision is still needed.

2.q: Why are time limits set for vibrating tools on site?
o: To slow production deliberately.
To help control vibration exposure.
To make batteries last longer.
To reduce tool theft risk.
To avoid daily inspections.
2.w: Exposure time limits help reduce the risk of hand-arm vibration injury.

n.0: The purpose is health protection, not delay.
n.2: Battery life is not the main reason.
n.3: The limits are not set for security reasons.
n.4: Inspections are still required.

2.q: What may indicate someone is not fit for work due to impairment?
o: Clean boots and gloves.
Early arrival to site.
Having lunch on time.
Slurred speech and unsteady movement.
Reading site notices carefully.
2.w: Slurred speech and poor balance may indicate impairment and should raise concern.

n.0: Clean PPE does not indicate impairment.
n.1: Arriving early is not a sign of impairment.
n.2: Lunch timing is unrelated.
n.4: Careful reading is not a warning sign.

2.q: Another worker removes a cover to drop materials through an opening and walks away. What should you do?
o: Get the opening protected again immediately
Leave it if no one is nearby
Stand beside it and continue your task
Place a tool near it as a warning
Wait until break time to mention it
2.w: Unprotected openings should be controlled immediately to prevent falls.

n.1: Someone may approach unexpectedly.
n.2: Standing nearby does not remove the hazard.
n.3: A tool is not adequate protection.
n.4: Delay leaves others at risk.

2.q: Workers are entering a noisy area. What should the employer do if noise cannot be reduced enough by other means?
o: Provide suitable hearing protection
Tell workers to cover ears with hands
Ignore short exposures completely
Play louder music to mask the noise
Move the signs further away
2.w: Where residual risk remains, suitable PPE such as hearing protection may be required.

n.1: Hands are not suitable protection.
n.2: Short exposure may still be harmful.
n.3: Masking sound does not reduce risk.
n.4: Sign placement does not control noise exposure.

2.q: You need to sweep a very dusty storeroom. Which is the best option?
o: Use suitable respiratory PPE for the dust level.
Use sunglasses instead.
Hold your breath while sweeping.
Work faster so exposure is shorter.
Only wear gloves.
2.w: Suitable respiratory PPE helps reduce inhalation of airborne dust during dusty work.

n.1: Sunglasses do not protect breathing.
n.2: Holding breath is not a safe control measure.
n.3: Speed does not remove the hazard.
n.4: Gloves do not protect lungs.

2.q: You are evacuating through a corridor and see someone injured but mobile. What should you do if safe?
o: Assist them toward the exit
Leave them without speaking
Carry them alone at speed
Send them back for first aid kit
Tell them to stay there
2.w: If safe, help them continue evacuating toward safety.

n.1: Ignoring them may leave them in danger.
n.2: Unsafe lifting may injure both people.
n.3: Do not send them away from the exit.
n.4: Leaving them behind may be unsafe.

2.q: You are carrying materials and approach a slip warning sign on a muddy ramp. Best action?
o: Reduce load or get help before using ramp
Keep same pace and hope for grip
Run to maintain balance
Look only at the load
Drag materials sideways quickly
2.w: Reduce manual handling difficulty and keep control on slippery ground.

n.1: Maintaining pace does not reduce slip risk.
n.2: Running increases loss of control.
n.3: You need to watch footing and surroundings.
n.4: Rushing with awkward movement is unsafe.

2.q: Before starting frequent lifting work, what is the best preparation?
o: Warm up muscles with light movement and stretches if appropriate
Start with the heaviest lift immediately
Sit still until the first load arrives
Lift quickly to warm up under load
Skip preparation if the load looks light
2.w: A sensible warm-up can prepare muscles and joints for physical work.

n.1: Heavy lifting without preparation can increase injury risk.
n.2: Remaining inactive does not prepare the body for work.
n.3: Using heavy work as a warm-up is poor practice.
n.4: Even light loads repeated often can cause strain.

2.q: Who should normally be contacted internally after raising an emergency alarm?
o: The supervisor, marshal or designated responsible person
Only a friend off site
A random passer-by
The payroll office first
No one else at all
2.w: Designated site personnel help coordinate the response.

n.1: Friends off site are not site coordinators.
n.2: Passers-by are not appropriate contacts.
n.3: Payroll is not the priority.
n.4: Further communication is often required.

2.q: Why is it important to report suspect asbestos immediately rather than at the end of the shift?
o: Because management prefers early paperwork
Because other workers may disturb it before the risk is controlled
Because the report will be cheaper to process in the morning
Because all suspect materials must be removed by labourers before handover
Because asbestos becomes harmless if it is reported within the same day
2.w: Immediate reporting helps prevent others from unknowingly disturbing the suspect material.

n.0: The key issue is safety, not paperwork timing.
n.2: Cost is not the reason for immediate reporting.
n.3: Labourers should not remove suspect asbestos.
n.4: Delay does not make asbestos harmless.

2.q: What is the best place to position a transformer during use?
o: On a stable dry area where it will not be damaged
Inside a puddle to cool it
Hanging by its cable
Balanced on loose rubble
In a walkway where everyone passes
2.w: Transformers should be placed on stable dry ground away from damage and trip risks.

n.1: Water increases electrical danger.
n.2: Hanging by cables can cause damage.
n.3: Loose rubble is unstable.
n.4: Walkways create hazards and risk impact.

2.q: A driver loses sight of the banksman during a reversing manoeuvre. What is the correct action?
o: Reverse slowly until the banksman reappears
Stop immediately and wait until clear contact is restored
Ask another worker to shout directions
Use the mirrors and continue
Sound the horn twice and carry on
2.w: If the banksman is no longer visible, the driver should stop until safe communication is restored.

n.0: Continuing without seeing the banksman is unsafe.
n.2: Unplanned shouted directions can be misunderstood.
n.3: Mirrors may not show all blind spots.
n.4: A horn does not replace clear visual control.

2.q: An entrant collapses inside a confined space. What is the best first action for a nearby worker?
o: Run in immediately to drag them out.
Shout and then continue your own task.
Raise the alarm and start the planned rescue procedure.
Wait quietly for the supervisor to return.
Turn off your detector to stop alarms.
2.w: Entering impulsively can create another casualty. Raise the alarm and follow the planned rescue arrangements.

n.0: Unplanned entry can expose you to the same hazard.
n.1: Ignoring a casualty is unacceptable.
n.3: Delay wastes critical rescue time.
n.4: Turning off alarms removes warnings and helps nobody.

2.q: You find a small but continuous leak under a generator. What should happen?
o: Ignore it until the next service.
Place cardboard under it and leave it.
Move the leak nearer a drain.
Only act if rain starts.
Contain it and report the equipment fault promptly.
2.w: Continuous leaks should be contained and reported so maintenance can stop further pollution.

n.0: Delays allow ongoing contamination.
n.1: Cardboard is not reliable spill control.
n.2: This increases environmental risk.
n.3: Action should not wait for weather changes.

2.q: You enter an area marked as a mandatory hearing protection zone. What must you do?
o: Only wear protection if machines are running.
Wait until someone reminds you.
Put on hearing protection before staying in the area.
Use protection only after one hour.
Ignore the sign if the area looks quiet.
2.w: Mandatory hearing zones require hearing protection to be worn as instructed.

n.0: Noise may start suddenly or already be harmful.
n.1: You should follow signage without waiting to be told.
n.3: Delaying use increases exposure.
n.4: The sign indicates controls are required regardless of appearance.

2.q: Two workers start pushing each other near moving plant as a joke. What should you do?
o: Tell them to stop and report unsafe behaviour if needed.
Join in so they calm down.
Ignore it because they are only joking.
Film it on your phone.
Wait to see if anyone gets hurt first.
2.w: Horseplay near plant creates serious risk. Unsafe behaviour should be stopped and reported through site procedures if necessary.

n.1: Joining in increases the risk.
n.2: Joking does not remove danger.
n.3: Recording it does not control the hazard.
n.4: Waiting may allow injury to occur.

2.q: Which sign suggests a ladder is set too shallow?
o: The feet are too far out
The ladder reaches well above the landing point, giving more to hold when stepping on or off
The stiles look straight and there is no obvious damage visible from ground level
The feet appear level on the ground and both side rails are taking load evenly
The ladder has rubber feet fitted and the rungs look clean and dry before climbing begins
2.w: If the feet are too far from the wall, the ladder may be too shallow and more likely to slip out.

n.1: Projecting above a landing point can be helpful and does not show the ladder is too shallow.
n.2: Straight stiles do not indicate the angle is wrong.
n.3: Even loading and level feet do not prove the angle is too shallow.
n.4: Clean rungs and rubber feet do not show that the angle is incorrect.

2.q: A scaffold board cracks under load but nobody falls. What does this count as?
o: A near miss that should be reported
Nothing because work continued
Only a maintenance issue next month
A private matter for one worker
Proof the scaffold is safe enough
2.w: A cracked board under load could have caused serious harm and is a near miss.

n.1: Continuing work does not remove the danger that occurred.
n.2: Urgent reporting is more appropriate than delay.
n.3: Others may also be at risk.
n.4: Failure signs show risk, not safety.

2.q: Why should you avoid removing one ear plug to talk while machinery is running?
o: One exposed ear can still be damaged
It improves hearing too much
It makes tools run faster
It prevents eye contact
It cleans the other ear
2.w: Partial protection can still leave one ear exposed to harmful noise.

n.1: The issue is exposure, not hearing improvement.
n.2: Hearing PPE does not affect machine speed.
n.3: Eye contact is unrelated.
n.4: Ear plugs do not clean ears.

2.q: Why should lifts usually not be used during evacuation?
o: They may fail or open into danger
They are slower than walking only
They are for managers only
They damage footwear
They are too expensive to run
2.w: Lifts may malfunction or stop at unsafe floors during an emergency.

n.1: Speed is not the main safety reason.
n.2: Lifts are not reserved for managers.
n.3: Footwear damage is irrelevant.
n.4: Running cost is not the issue.

2.q: You notice a green exit sign pointing right, but a temporary barrier blocks that route. What is the best action?
o: Ignore the barrier and squeeze through
Report it and use another safe signed route
Remove all barriers yourself regardless of risk
Wait there for instructions only
Assume the sign is wrong
2.w: Use another safe route and report the obstruction so it can be corrected.

n.0: Forcing through barriers may be unsafe.
n.2: Do not create extra risk by moving barriers unsafely.
n.3: Waiting may delay safe evacuation.
n.4: The issue may be the barrier, not the sign.

2.q: Which sequence is safest for a two-person lift?
o: Assess load, agree plan, take grip, lift on command
Grip first, lift randomly, discuss route later
One lifts, one watches, then swap
Carry first, then decide where to place it
Twist it upright, then ask for help
2.w: Assessment, planning, grip and coordinated lifting is the safest sequence.

n.1: Random lifting risks imbalance and confusion.
n.2: Both workers should participate together.
n.3: Placement should be planned before moving.
n.4: Help should be arranged before lifting.

2.q: What is the main purpose of a site first aid room where provided?
o: To provide a suitable place for treatment and care
To store everyone’s lunch
To hold disciplinary meetings
To park small tools overnight
To replace all hospitals
2.w: A first aid room supports treatment in a clean, organised environment.

n.1: It is not intended as a lunch storage area.
n.2: Its purpose is medical support, not discipline.
n.3: Tool storage is not the main function.
n.4: It does not replace hospitals or emergency services.

2.q: If respiratory protective equipment is required for dusty cutting, when should it be worn?
o: Only after coughing starts
Before exposure begins and throughout the task
Only during breaks
After the room clears
Only when supervisors visit
2.w: RPE must be worn before entering exposure and during the dusty task.

n.0: Waiting until symptoms start is too late.
n.2: Breaks are not the main exposure period.
n.3: After the room clears gives no protection during work.
n.4: Use depends on risk, not supervision.

2.q: Which sign most strongly suggests internal cable damage even if no wires are visible?
o: A clean plug top
A slight twist in the lead
A section that gets unusually hot in use
A new tag on the tool
A bright coloured outer sheath
2.w: Unusual heating can indicate internal damage, poor connection, or insulation failure and should be treated as a defect.

n.0: A clean plug does not show internal damage.
n.1: A slight twist alone is not the clearest warning sign.
n.3: A tag does not prove the lead is currently safe.
n.4: Colour does not indicate condition.

2.q: Which worker position is usually safest for a banksman guiding a dumper in reverse?
o: Directly behind the dumper
Where the driver can clearly see them and clear of the path
Between the dumper and a wall
On the rear step
Next to the rear wheel
2.w: The banksman should be visible to the driver while staying out of the vehicle path.

n.0: Behind the dumper is a blind spot.
n.2: This creates a trapping hazard.
n.3: Riding the rear step is unsafe.
n.4: Standing by wheels risks crushing.

2.q: Why should spoil heaps be kept away from the edge of a trench?
o: To make the trench look tidy
To reduce extra weight on the sides and stop material falling in
To keep tools cleaner
To make climbing out easier
To create more noise barriers
2.w: Spoil heaps near the edge increase pressure on trench sides and can fall into the excavation.

n.0: Appearance is not the main safety reason.
n.2: Tool cleanliness is unrelated.
n.3: Access is important, but load on the sides is the key issue.
n.4: Noise control is unrelated.

2.q: Why is waste segregation important on a construction site?
o: It makes skips heavier.
It helps recycling and reduces disposal costs.
It allows all waste to go into one skip.
It removes the need for labels.
It means collections are never needed.
2.w: Separating waste streams improves recycling and can reduce disposal charges.

n.0: Skip weight is not the purpose of segregation.
n.2: Segregation is the opposite of mixing waste.
n.3: Labels are still useful for correct disposal.
n.4: Waste collections are still required.

2.q: What is the best reason to keep hearing protectors fitted properly in a noisy area?
o: They make tools quieter for everyone.
They remove the need for maintenance.
They guarantee zero noise reaches the ear.
They are only needed for visitors.
Poor fit can reduce protection significantly.
2.w: Incorrectly fitted hearing protection may not provide the expected level of protection.

n.0: They protect the wearer rather than quietening tools for all.
n.1: Tool maintenance is still required.
n.2: No protector guarantees zero noise exposure.
n.3: Anyone exposed may need protection, not only visitors.

2.q: A section of fencing has fallen, leaving direct access from the pavement into the site. What is the best action?
o: Wait until the next inspection.
Stand nearby if you have time.
Reinstate protection or secure the area immediately and report it.
Put tools in front of the gap.
Assume nobody will enter.
2.w: Broken fencing creating public access should be secured promptly and reported.

n.0: Delay leaves the public exposed to risk.
n.1: Standing nearby is not reliable protection.
n.3: Loose tools are not suitable barriers.
n.4: You should not rely on assumptions where access exists.

2.q: You must move across a fragile roof section. What is the best action?
o: Walk on the strongest-looking sheets only
Use the planned safe route or crawling boards provided
Follow another worker's footsteps exactly
Unclip temporarily to move more easily
Move quickly to reduce time on the roof
2.w: Fragile roofs should only be crossed using the planned safe access system such as boards or platforms.

n.0: Appearance does not confirm strength.
n.2: Following footsteps does not guarantee safety.
n.3: Removing protection increases the risk.
n.4: Speed does not make the surface safer.

2.q: You are required to wear eye protection for a task. What is the employer's duty?
o: Provide suitable PPE where needed
Tell workers to buy any glasses themselves
Provide PPE only after an accident
Allow workers to share damaged PPE
Replace PPE with warning signs only
2.w: Where risks remain, employers should provide suitable PPE.

n.1: Passing all responsibility to workers may be unsuitable and non-compliant.
n.2: PPE should be available before incidents happen.
n.3: Damaged shared PPE may be ineffective or unhygienic.
n.4: Signs do not replace required PPE.

2.q: You are asked to enter an area beneath scaffolders for two minutes to collect tools. What is the best action?
o: Wear your hard hat correctly and follow site controls before entering
Go quickly without it because the task is brief
Use a baseball cap since it is lighter
Wait until no one is watching and enter
Carry the hard hat in case you need it
2.w: Short duration does not remove risk; use required PPE and controls.

n.1: Brief exposure can still result in injury.
n.2: A cap is not industrial head protection.
n.3: Avoiding supervision does not reduce hazards.
n.4: Carrying it gives no protection.

2.q: A permit has expired but the weld is nearly complete. What should you do?
o: Finish quickly anyway
Stop work and have the permit revalidated or renewed
Ignore the time shown
Ask a friend verbally
Hide the permit
2.w: Expired permits should not be ignored. Work should stop until properly reauthorised.

n.0: Nearly complete work still needs valid controls.
n.2: Permit times are part of control measures.
n.3: Informal approval may be inadequate.
n.4: Concealing documents is unacceptable.

2.q: A gloves-must-be-worn sign is beside sharp sheet materials. What is the safest action?
o: Use suitable protective gloves
Handle carefully with bare hands
Use only one glove
Ask someone else to lift them
Ignore it for small pieces
2.w: The sign requires gloves to reduce hand injury risk.

n.1: Bare hands remain exposed.
n.2: One glove leaves one hand unprotected.
n.3: Another person does not remove the requirement.
n.4: Small items can still cause injury.

2.q: Which action is best if lifting tasks are repeated all day?
o: Rotate tasks where possible to vary movements
Use the same posture without pause
Lift faster each hour to keep pace
Carry extra loads to finish early
Ignore tiredness until the shift ends
2.w: Task rotation can reduce repeated stress on the same muscles and joints.

n.1: Constant repetition can increase strain risk.
n.2: Increasing speed may worsen fatigue.
n.3: Extra loads may increase risk.
n.4: Fatigue should not be ignored.

2.q: You see a stack of boards leaning dangerously but still standing. What is the best immediate action?
o: Report it and keep people clear of the area
Leave it because nothing has fallen yet
Take one board away to test stability
Walk past quickly and say nothing
Wait for break time to mention it
2.w: Unsafe stacking is a near miss risk. Report it immediately and prevent access if safe to do so.

n.1: The danger exists before anything falls.
n.2: Interfering could worsen the instability.
n.3: Ignoring hazards exposes others to risk.
n.4: Delayed reporting is poor control of an immediate risk.

2.q: You are asked to remove a small panel from an older building, but no one can confirm what it is made from. What should you do?
o: Take it off slowly with minimum force
Score round it first to limit dust
Stop and ask for the material to be checked before disturbing it
Use a stronger tool so the job is over quickly
Wear two dust masks and carry on with the removal
2.w: If the material is unknown in an older building, it should be checked before any disturbance takes place.

n.0: Slow removal still disturbs the material.
n.1: Scoring it first can release fibres if it contains asbestos.
n.3: A stronger tool may increase breakage and dust release.
n.4: Extra masks do not make it acceptable to disturb suspect asbestos.
